decks.title: Biomolecules — Part 1: Chemical constituents and proteins
goals: Explain how the chemical composition of a tissue is analysed
Describe amino acids, lipids, nucleotides and metabolites
Describe peptide bonds, the structure of proteins and their functions

slides.heading: Biomolecules
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what living tissue is made of, from small molecules to proteins.

visual.alt: Flow of the analysis of a living tissue into acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions

slides.narration: To find out what a tissue is made of, chemists grind it in trichloroacetic acid and filter the slurry. Thousands of small organic compounds pass into the filtrate, while large molecules stay behind in the retentate. Each part is then analysed.

slides.heading: Elements in living and non-living matter
slides.body_md: All the elements of the earth’s crust occur in living tissue, but in very different proportions (percent by weight).

visual.alt: Table comparing elements in the earth’s crust and the human body

slides.narration: Living matter is especially rich in carbon and hydrogen, while silicon, abundant in rocks, is almost absent from the body. Analysis also reveals inorganic ions such as sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium, and compounds such as phosphate and sulphate.

slides.heading: Amino acids
slides.body_md: Amino acids have an **amino group** and an acidic **carboxyl group** on the same carbon, the **alpha carbon**. The variable **R group** decides which of the 20 amino acids it is.

slides.narration: Amino acids can be acidic, like glutamic acid, basic, like lysine, or neutral, like valine; tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan are aromatic. Their amino and carboxyl groups are ionisable, so their structure changes with pH, forming a zwitterion at a particular pH.

slides.narration: Palmitic acid has sixteen carbons and arachidonic acid twenty, counting the carboxyl carbon. Fatty acids are saturated or unsaturated. Glycerol joined to one, two or three fatty acids gives glycerides; oils stay liquid in winter, fats are solid. Phospholipids such as lecithin build cell membranes.

slides.heading: Nitrogen bases, nucleosides and nucleotides
slides.body_md: Heterocyclic **nitrogen bases** join a sugar to form **nucleosides**; adding a **phosphate** gives **nucleotides**.

visual.alt: Table of bases, nucleosides and nucleotides

slides.narration: Adenine with a sugar is adenosine, a nucleoside. When a phosphate group is also esterified to the sugar, it becomes adenylic acid, a nucleotide. Nucleotides are the building blocks of the nucleic acids, DNA and RNA.

slides.heading: Primary and secondary metabolites
slides.body_md: **Primary metabolites** (amino acids, sugars, nucleotides) have known roles in normal physiology. **Secondary metabolites**, mainly from plants, fungi and microbes, are often useful to people.

visual.alt: Table of kinds of secondary metabolites with examples

slides.narration: We do not yet understand the role of most secondary metabolites in the organisms that make them, but many are important to human welfare as drugs, dyes, flavours and raw materials such as rubber.

slides.heading: Biomacromolecules
slides.body_md: Compounds in the acid-soluble pool are **micromolecules** (below 1000 daltons). **Macromolecules** — proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides — are above ten thousand daltons and form the acid-insoluble fraction. Lipids, though small, also appear there because membranes break into insoluble vesicles.

visual.alt: Table of the average composition of cells

slides.narration: Water makes up most of a cell. Among the rest, proteins are the largest share. The acid-soluble pool roughly represents the cytoplasm, while the macromolecules of the cytoplasm and organelles make up the acid-insoluble fraction.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: water and dry mass
slides.body_md: A 40 g sample of fresh leaf loses 85 percent of its mass on drying. What is its dry mass?
bullets: Dry fraction $= 100 - 85 = 15$ percent.
Dry mass $= 40 \times \dfrac{15}{100} = 6$ g.
The dry mass contains the organic compounds and minerals; water lies within the 70 to 90 percent range.

visual.alt: Worked table: dry mass 6 g

slides.narration: If eighty-five percent is water, fifteen percent is left. Fifteen percent of forty grams is six grams. That small dry mass holds all the proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and minerals of the sample.

slides.narration: Each time two amino acids join, one molecule of water is removed. A protein is a heteropolymer of up to twenty kinds of amino acids. Amino acids that our body cannot make are essential and must come from the diet; the rest are non-essential.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting bonds and mass
slides.body_md: Alanine has a molecular mass of 89 daltons and water 18 daltons. Find the mass of the dipeptide alanylalanine, and the number of peptide bonds in an unbranched chain of 50 amino acids.
bullets: Dipeptide: $2 \times 89 - 18 = 160$ daltons.
Chain of 50: $50 - 1 = 49$ peptide bonds, and as many water molecules released.
The same rule, one bond fewer than units, holds for glycosidic bonds in a polysaccharide chain.

visual.alt: Worked table: dipeptide 160 daltons; 49 bonds in a chain of fifty

slides.narration: Joining two alanines removes one water, so subtract eighteen from one hundred and seventy-eight to get one hundred and sixty. In any unbranched chain, the number of bonds is one fewer than the number of units.

slides.narration: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, from the N-terminal to the C-terminal end. Parts of the chain coil into right-handed helices, the secondary structure. The chain then folds upon itself like a woollen ball, the tertiary structure. Several chains may assemble into a quaternary structure, as in haemoglobin with two alpha and two beta subunits.

slides.heading: Functions of proteins
slides.body_md: Proteins carry nutrients across membranes, fight infection, act as hormones and enzymes, and build structures. **Collagen** is the most abundant protein in the animal world, and **RuBisCO** in the whole biosphere.

rows: Sensory reception of smell, taste and hormones

visual.alt: Table of proteins and their functions

slides.narration: Almost every job in a cell is done by a protein. Enzymes speed reactions, hormones carry signals, antibodies defend the body, receptors detect smells and tastes, and transport proteins move substances such as glucose into cells.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Grinding in trichloroacetic acid separates an acid-soluble pool (micromolecules) from an acid-insoluble fraction (macromolecules).
Amino acids: alpha carbon with H, amino, carboxyl and R groups; acidic, basic, neutral, aromatic.
Lipids: fatty acids (palmitic 16 C), glycerol, glycerides, phospholipids (lecithin).
Bases → nucleosides → nucleotides; primary and secondary metabolites.
Proteins: peptide bonds; primary to quaternary structure; collagen and RuBisCO; varied functions.

visual.alt: Summary table of building blocks and their polymers

slides.narration: To recap: a cell is mostly water, with small molecules in the acid-soluble pool and large ones in the insoluble fraction. Amino acids join by peptide bonds into proteins, whose four levels of structure give each protein its shape and function.

slides.narration: Polysaccharides store energy and build walls and shells. Nucleic acids carry hereditary information. And enzymes, most of which are proteins, make the reactions of metabolism happen fast enough to support life.

slides.heading: Kinds of polysaccharides
slides.body_md: Polysaccharides can be homopolymers or heteropolymers.

rows: Plant cell walls, paper, cotton; does not hold iodine
Plant energy store; helices hold iodine and turn blue

slides.narration: Starch forms helical regions that trap iodine, which is why it turns blue-black. Cellulose has no such helices, so cotton and paper do not. Chitin is a complex polysaccharide built from chemically modified sugars such as glucosamine.

slides.body_md: Nucleotides are joined by **phosphodiester bonds**: the phosphate links the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ carbon of the next. Watson and Crick described DNA as a **double helix**.

slides.narration: The two strands run in opposite directions and are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases: adenine with thymine by two bonds, guanine with cytosine by three. In the common B form of DNA, one full turn contains ten base pairs and is three point four nanometres long.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: measuring a stretch of DNA
slides.body_md: A B-DNA segment has 150 base pairs. How many turns and how long is it? A smaller piece with 3 A–T and 7 G–C pairs: how many hydrogen bonds?
bullets: Turns $= \dfrac{150}{10} = 15$; length $= 15 \times 3.4 = 51$ nm.
Hydrogen bonds $= 3 \times 2 + 7 \times 3 = 27$.
More G–C pairs mean more hydrogen bonds, so the strands are harder to separate.

visual.alt: Worked table: 15 turns, 51 nanometres, 27 hydrogen bonds

slides.narration: Ten base pairs make one turn, so one hundred and fifty pairs make fifteen turns, each three point four nanometres long, about fifty-one nanometres in all. For hydrogen bonds, count two for each A and T pair and three for each G and C pair.

slides.heading: Enzymes: what they are
slides.body_md: Almost all enzymes are **proteins**; some nucleic acids, **ribozymes**, also act as enzymes. The tertiary structure forms an **active site**, a crevice or pocket for the substrate. Rate of a reaction is the amount of product formed per unit time.

rows: Work best at high temperatures and pressures
Damaged at high temperatures, say above 40 °C
About 600,000 molecules of carbonic acid a second, against about 200 an hour without it: about ten million times faster
Rate roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise

visual.alt: Table of features of enzymes compared with other catalysts

slides.narration: Carbonic anhydrase shows how powerful enzymes are. Without it, carbon dioxide and water form only a couple of hundred molecules of carbonic acid in an hour. With it, six hundred thousand form every second. Metabolic pathways, such as the ten steps that turn glucose into pyruvic acid, are chains of such catalysed reactions.

slides.heading: How enzymes speed up reactions
slides.body_md: To become product, the substrate must pass through a high-energy **transition state**. The energy needed is the **activation energy**. Enzymes **lower** this barrier.

slides.narration: Below the optimum temperature an enzyme is only temporarily inactive, but high temperature denatures the protein. Activity also falls on either side of the optimum pH. With more substrate the rate climbs until every enzyme molecule is busy; adding still more substrate then has no effect.

slides.heading: Inhibitors
slides.body_md: A chemical that shuts off enzyme activity is an **inhibitor**. A **competitive inhibitor** closely resembles the substrate and competes for the substrate-binding site.

visual.alt: Flow of malonate competing with succinate for the active site of succinic dehydrogenase

slides.narration: Malonate looks so like succinate that it occupies the active site of succinic dehydrogenase, which then cannot act on succinate. Competitive inhibitors of this kind are often used to control bacterial pathogens.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading rates
slides.body_md: An uncatalysed reaction runs at 8 units per minute at 30 °C. Estimate its rate at 20 °C. An enzyme reaction has formed 2.4 units of product at 4 minutes and 6.0 units at 10 minutes. Find its average rate over this interval.
bullets: Uncatalysed: a 10 °C fall halves the rate: $\dfrac{8}{2} = 4$ units per minute.
Enzyme: $\dfrac{6.0 - 2.4}{10 - 4} = \dfrac{3.6}{6} = 0.6$ units per minute.
Rate is the change in product divided by the time taken.

visual.alt: Worked table: rates 4 and 0.6 units per minute

slides.narration: For the uncatalysed reaction, cooling by ten degrees halves the rate, giving four. For the enzyme, three point six units were made in six minutes, so the average rate is zero point six units per minute.

slides.heading: Classification of enzymes
slides.body_md: Enzymes are divided into **six classes**, each with subclasses, by the type of reaction they catalyse.

rows: Transfer of a group other than hydrogen between substrates
Hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds
Removal of groups by means other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds
Inter-conversion of optical, geometric or positional isomers
Linking two compounds, forming C–O, C–S, C–N or P–O bonds

visual.alt: Table of the six classes of enzymes

slides.narration: Ask what the enzyme does to its substrate. Moving hydrogen or electrons means an oxidoreductase; moving another group, a transferase; splitting with water, a hydrolase; removing a group to leave a double bond, a lyase; rearranging atoms, an isomerase; and joining two molecules, a ligase.

slides.heading: Cofactors
slides.body_md: Many enzymes need a **non-protein cofactor**; the protein part is the **apoenzyme**. Activity is lost when the cofactor is removed.

rows: Organic, tightly bound to the apoenzyme
Organic, bound only during catalysis; often contains a vitamin
Forms coordination bonds at the active site

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of cofactors with examples

slides.narration: Peroxidase and catalase break hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen with the help of haem, which is part of their active site. Coenzymes attach only while the reaction happens, and many are made from vitamins. Metal ions such as zinc bind both enzyme and substrate.

slides.heading: Quick check: coenzymes
slides.body_md: Which vitamin is found in the coenzymes NAD and NADP?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is one of the B vitamins.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Polysaccharides: glycosidic bonds; cellulose, starch, glycogen, inulin, chitin; starch holds iodine.
Nucleic acids: nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds; DNA double helix, A–T two and G–C three hydrogen bonds; 10 base pairs and 3.4 nm per turn.
Enzymes: mostly proteins (also ribozymes); active site; lower activation energy; induced fit.
Activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration (Vmax); competitive inhibitors such as malonate.
Six classes; cofactors: prosthetic groups, coenzymes, metal ions.

rows: Base pairs of two DNA strands

visual.alt: Summary table of bonds in biomolecules

slides.narration: To recap: sugars join by glycosidic bonds, nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds, and two DNA strands by hydrogen bonds. Enzymes lower the activation energy of reactions; they work best at an optimum temperature and pH, can be saturated with substrate and blocked by look-alike inhibitors.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain the **iodine test** difference between starch and cellulose.
Count **hydrogen bonds** and **turns** in DNA carefully.
Draw and label the **activation energy** diagram.
Learn the **six enzyme classes** and **three cofactors** with examples.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Know why starch turns blue with iodine but cellulose does not. Practise counting hydrogen bonds and turns in DNA. Draw the activation energy diagram neatly. And learn the six classes of enzymes and the three kinds of cofactors with one example each.

sections.heading: 1. Chemical constituents of living cells
sections.body_md:
**How to analyse.** A living tissue (a vegetable or a piece of liver) is ground in **trichloroacetic acid** with a mortar and pestle to a thick slurry and strained through cheesecloth. The **filtrate** is the **acid-soluble pool**; the **retentate** is the **acid-insoluble fraction**. Thousands of organic compounds are found in the acid-soluble pool. Elemental analysis shows that living matter has the same elements as the earth’s crust, but in different proportions: carbon and hydrogen are relatively more abundant in living organisms (carbon 18.5 percent of the human body against 0.03 percent of the crust; silicon 27.7 percent of the crust, negligible in the body). Inorganic constituents include ions of sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium, water, and compounds such as sodium chloride, calcium carbonate, phosphate and sulphate.

**Amino acids** are organic compounds with an **amino group** and an acidic **carboxyl group** as substituents on the same carbon, the **α-carbon**; they are substituted methanes with four substituents: hydrogen, carboxyl, amino and a variable **R group**. R is H in **glycine**, a methyl group in **alanine** and hydroxymethyl in **serine**. Based on the number of amino and carboxyl groups, amino acids are **acidic** (glutamic acid), **basic** (lysine) or **neutral** (valine); **aromatic** amino acids include **tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan**. Because the –NH2 and –COOH groups are ionisable, the structure of amino acids changes with pH, forming a **zwitterion** at a particular pH.

**Lipids** are generally water-insoluble. They may be simple **fatty acids**: a carboxyl group attached to an R group (methyl, ethyl or a chain of 1 to 19 carbons). **Palmitic acid** has 16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon; **arachidonic acid** has 20. Fatty acids are **saturated** (no double bond) or **unsaturated** (one or more C=C bonds). **Glycerol** is trihydroxy propane; fatty acids esterified with glycerol give **monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides** (fats and oils, by melting point: oils such as gingelly oil have lower melting points and stay liquid in winter). **Phospholipids**, such as **lecithin**, contain phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound and occur in cell membranes; neural tissue has lipids with more complex structures.

**Nitrogen bases, nucleosides, nucleotides.** Heterocyclic rings: **adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine**. Base + sugar = **nucleoside** (adenosine, guanosine, thymidine, uridine, cytidine); with a phosphate esterified to the sugar = **nucleotide** (adenylic, thymidylic, guanylic, uridylic and cytidylic acids). Nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA consist of nucleotides only.

**Metabolites.** **Primary metabolites** (amino acids, sugars and others) have identifiable functions in normal physiology. **Secondary metabolites** — pigments (carotenoids, anthocyanins), alkaloids (morphine, codeine), terpenoids, essential oils (lemon grass oil), toxins (abrin, ricin), lectins (concanavalin A), drugs (vinblastin, curcumin), polymeric substances (rubber, gums, cellulose) — occur mainly in plants, fungi and microbes; many are useful to human welfare.

sections.heading: 2. Biomacromolecules and proteins
sections.body_md:
Compounds in the acid-soluble pool have molecular weights of about **18 to 800 daltons**; those below 1000 Da are **micromolecules**. The acid-insoluble fraction has **proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids**; apart from lipids, these are above **ten thousand daltons** — the **biomacromolecules**. Lipids (below 800 Da) appear in the insoluble fraction because grinding breaks membranes into **vesicles that are not water-soluble**. The acid-soluble pool roughly represents the cytoplasmic composition. Average composition of cells (percent of total mass): **water 70–90, proteins 10–15, carbohydrates 3, lipids 2, nucleic acids 5–7, ions 1**.

**Proteins** are **polypeptides**: linear chains of amino acids linked by **peptide bonds**, formed between the **carboxyl group** of one amino acid and the **amino group** of the next with **loss of water** (dehydration). Proteins are **heteropolymers** of up to **20** kinds of amino acids. **Essential amino acids** must come from the diet; **non-essential** ones the body makes. Functions: transport across membranes, defence (antibodies fight infectious agents), hormones (insulin), enzymes (trypsin), structure (**collagen**, intercellular ground substance), receptors (smell, taste, hormones), **GLUT-4** (glucose transport into cells). **Collagen** is the most abundant protein in the animal world and **RuBisCO** in the whole biosphere.

**Structure of proteins.**
- **Primary:** the sequence of amino acids; the first is the **N-terminal** and the last the **C-terminal** amino acid.
- **Secondary:** parts of the chain arranged as a **helix** — only **right-handed** helices are observed in proteins — while other regions fold in other forms.
- **Tertiary:** the long chain folded upon itself like a hollow woollen ball, giving a 3-D view needed for many biological activities.
- **Quaternary:** an assembly of more than one polypeptide (subunit), as in adult human **haemoglobin** with **two α and two β** subunits.

sections.heading: 3. Polysaccharides and nucleic acids
sections.body_md:
**Polysaccharides** are long chains of sugars, the monosaccharides being joined by **glycosidic bonds** formed by dehydration between two carbon atoms of adjacent sugars. **Cellulose** is a **homopolymer** of glucose; **starch** is the store house of energy in plants and **glycogen** in animals; **inulin** is a polymer of **fructose**. In a polysaccharide chain such as glycogen, the **right end** is the **reducing end** and the **left end** the **non-reducing end**; glycogen is branched. **Starch** forms helical secondary structures that can hold **iodine** (blue colour); **cellulose** does not contain complex helices and cannot hold iodine. Plant cell walls are cellulose; paper from plant pulp and cotton fibre is cellulosic. **Complex polysaccharides** have amino-sugars and chemically modified sugars (glucosamine, N-acetyl galactosamine) as building blocks; the exoskeleton of arthropods is **chitin**, a heteropolymer.

**Nucleic acids** are **polynucleotides**. A nucleotide has a **heterocyclic nitrogenous base**, a **monosaccharide** and **phosphoric acid**. **Adenine and guanine** are substituted **purines**; **cytosine, uracil and thymine** are substituted **pyrimidines**. The sugar is **ribose** (in RNA) or **2′-deoxyribose** (in DNA). The **phosphate** links the **3′ carbon** of one sugar to the **5′ carbon** of the next: an ester bond on each side, the **phosphodiester bond**.

**DNA double helix** (Watson and Crick): two strands **antiparallel**, held by **hydrogen bonds** between bases; **A pairs with T** by **two** hydrogen bonds and **G with C** by **three**. In **B-DNA**, one full turn has **10 base pairs** and a pitch of **3.4 nm** (34 Å), so the rise per base pair is 0.34 nm.

key_terms.definition_md: Bond between two adjacent monosaccharides, formed by dehydration.

sections.heading: 4. Enzymes
sections.body_md:
**Nature.** Almost all enzymes are **proteins**; some nucleic acids that behave like enzymes are **ribozymes**. An enzyme has a **tertiary structure** whose backbone folds to form **crevices or pockets**, the **active site**, into which the substrate fits. **Inorganic catalysts** work efficiently at **high temperatures and pressures**; enzymes get damaged at high temperatures (say above **40 °C**), but enzymes from organisms of very hot habitats (hot vents, sulphur springs) are stable at **80–90 °C**.

**Rates.** A physical change alters shape without breaking bonds; a chemical reaction breaks and forms bonds. Rate = amount of product formed per unit time ($\frac{\delta P}{\delta t}$). For chemical reactions the rate roughly **doubles or halves for every 10 °C** change. Catalysed reactions are vastly faster: **carbonic anhydrase** makes about **600,000** molecules of carbonic acid a **second**, against about **200** an **hour** uncatalysed — about **10 million times** faster. A **metabolic pathway** is a chain of such steps; glucose becomes two molecules of pyruvic acid in ten enzyme-catalysed steps, then lactic acid in skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions or ethanol in yeast during fermentation.

**How enzymes work.** The substrate must pass through a high-energy **transition state**; the difference between its average energy and the transition state is the **activation energy**. Even if the product has less energy than the substrate (no heat needs to be supplied), the barrier remains; enzymes **lower** it. Steps: (1) substrate binds the **active site**; (2) binding **induces** the enzyme to change shape and fit more tightly (**induced fit**), forming the **ES complex**; (3) the active site breaks chemical bonds of the substrate, forming the **EP complex**; (4) products are released and the enzyme is free again.

**Factors.** Each enzyme has an **optimum temperature** and **optimum pH**, with activity declining on either side; **low temperature** keeps enzymes temporarily inactive, **high temperature** destroys activity by **denaturing** the protein. Velocity rises with **substrate concentration** and reaches a maximum, **Vmax**, because enzyme molecules are fewer than substrate molecules and become saturated. An **inhibitor** shuts off activity; a **competitive inhibitor** closely resembles the substrate and competes for the binding site — **malonate** inhibits **succinic dehydrogenase** by resembling **succinate**. Competitive inhibitors are often used to control bacterial pathogens.

**Classification (six classes):** **oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases** (oxidation–reduction between two substrates); **transferases** (transfer of a group other than hydrogen); **hydrolases** (hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds); **lyases** (removal of groups by means other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds); **isomerases** (inter-conversion of optical, geometric or positional isomers); **ligases** (linking two compounds, e.g. forming C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds).

**Cofactors** are non-protein constituents that make an enzyme catalytically active; the protein part is the **apoenzyme**, and activity is lost if the cofactor is removed. **Prosthetic groups** are organic and tightly bound (**haem** in **peroxidase** and **catalase**, which break hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen). **Coenzymes** are organic and bound only transiently during catalysis; many contain **vitamins** (**NAD and NADP** contain **niacin**). **Metal ions** form coordination bonds at the active site (**zinc** in **carboxypeptidase**).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying all enzymes are proteins (ribozymes are nucleic acids).
- Placing lipids in the acid-soluble pool because they are small.
- Confusing nucleosides (base + sugar) with nucleotides (base + sugar + phosphate).
- Writing that cellulose turns blue with iodine (starch does).
- Saying enzymes change the energy of the product; they lower the activation energy.
- Giving collagen as the most abundant protein of the biosphere (that is RuBisCO; collagen leads in animals).
- Counting peptide bonds equal to the number of amino acids (it is one fewer per chain).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name an amino acid, polysaccharide, enzyme class, cofactor or bond; read a pH or temperature optimum.
- 2–3-mark answers: analysis with trichloroacetic acid; metabolites; levels of protein structure; polysaccharides; steps of enzyme action; cofactors; saturation and inhibition.
- 5-mark answers: chemical constituents; biomacromolecules; enzyme action and factors; classification and cofactors; evaluating a temperature prediction.
- Case-based items: a tissue analysis, a four-chain protein, a pH series or a competitive inhibitor, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: A student grinds a piece of liver in trichloroacetic acid and filters it. Which substances will she find mainly in the filtrate (the acid-soluble pool)?

options.text_md: Small molecules such as amino acids, sugars and nucleotides

questions.solution_md: The acid-soluble filtrate holds micromolecules below about 1000 daltons; macromolecules stay in the retentate — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Lipids have molecular weights below 800 daltons, yet they turn up in the acid-insoluble fraction when tissue is ground. What explains this?

options.text_md: Grinding breaks membranes into vesicles that are not water-soluble, and they separate with the insoluble pool
Lipids join with proteins to form polymers above 10000 daltons
Lipids are destroyed by the acid
Lipids dissolve only in the filtrate

questions.solution_md: Membrane fragments form insoluble vesicles that go with the retentate, though lipids are not true macromolecules — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Analyses give carbon as about 18.5 percent of the human body by weight but only 0.03 percent of the earth’s crust, while silicon is 27.7 percent of the crust and negligible in the body. What does this suggest?

options.text_md: Living matter has the same elements in the same proportions as the crust
Silicon is the main element of biomolecules
Carbon is absent from non-living matter
Living matter selectively builds its compounds mainly from carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen

questions.solution_md: All elements of the crust occur in living tissue, but in very different proportions; carbon and hydrogen are relatively far more abundant in living matter — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the amino acid serine, the R group is
questions.solution_md: Glycine has H, alanine a methyl group and serine a hydroxymethyl group as R — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an aromatic amino acid?
questions.solution_md: Tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan are aromatic — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why does the structure of an amino acid change when it is placed in solutions of different pH?

options.text_md: Its amino and carboxyl groups are ionisable and gain or lose protons, so a zwitterionic form exists at a particular pH
Its R group breaks off in acid
Its alpha carbon changes into silicon
It joins with other amino acids to form proteins

questions.solution_md: The ionisable –NH2 and –COOH groups change their charge with pH — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Palmitic acid has

options.text_md: 20 carbon atoms, including the carboxyl carbon
3 carbon atoms and three hydroxyl groups
16 carbon atoms, including the carboxyl carbon
16 carbon atoms plus a separate carboxyl carbon

questions.solution_md: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons counting the carboxyl carbon; arachidonic acid has 20 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Lecithin, a lipid found in cell membranes, is a

options.text_md: phospholipid, with phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound

questions.solution_md: Lecithin is a phospholipid; membranes have phospholipids — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Adenine joined to a sugar is adenosine. What is the compound called when a phosphate group is also esterified to the sugar?
questions.solution_md: Base + sugar is a nucleoside; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide, such as adenylic acid — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The anticancer drug vinblastin is extracted from a plant, which does not need it for its basic metabolism. In plant chemistry, vinblastin is classed as
questions.solution_md: Compounds such as drugs, alkaloids, pigments and toxins with no known role in normal physiology are secondary metabolites — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lipids are found in the acid-insoluble fraction of a ground tissue.

**Reason (R):** The molecular weights of lipids do not exceed about 800 daltons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but a low molecular weight would put lipids in the soluble pool; they appear in the insoluble fraction because membranes form insoluble vesicles — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Glycerol, which combines with fatty acids to form fats, is chemically trihydroxy ______.
questions.solution_md: Trihydroxy propane.

questions.stem_md: Amino acids are substituted methanes in which four groups occupy the valencies of the ______ carbon.
questions.solution_md: The alpha (α) carbon.

questions.stem_md: How is the chemical composition of a living tissue analysed using trichloroacetic acid?

answer.model_answer_md: The tissue is **ground in trichloroacetic acid** to a slurry and **filtered**. The **filtrate** (acid-soluble pool) holds **micromolecules** below 1000 daltons; the **retentate** (acid-insoluble fraction) holds **macromolecules** — proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides — and membrane lipids. Each is then analysed separately.

questions.solution_md: Grinding, filtrate, retentate.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between primary and secondary metabolites, with two examples of secondary metabolites.

answer.model_answer_md: **Primary metabolites** such as amino acids, sugars and nucleotides have **known roles** in normal physiological processes. **Secondary metabolites**, found mainly in plants, fungi and microbes, have no clear role in the organism’s basic physiology but are often useful to people: **alkaloids** (morphine, codeine), **pigments** (carotenoids, anthocyanins), **toxins** (abrin, ricin), **essential oils** and **rubber**.

questions.solution_md: Roles and examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of an amino acid and classify amino acids by the nature of their R groups, giving examples.

answer.model_answer_md: An amino acid has an **alpha carbon** bearing a **hydrogen**, an **amino group** (–NH2), a **carboxyl group** (–COOH) and a variable **R group**; it is a substituted methane. The **R group** decides which of the **20** amino acids it is: H in **glycine**, methyl in **alanine**, hydroxymethyl in **serine**. By the number of amino and carboxyl groups, amino acids are **acidic** (glutamic acid), **basic** (lysine) or **neutral** (valine); **aromatic** ones include **tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan**.

questions.solution_md: Structure; classes.

questions.stem_md: Describe fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids, and distinguish fats from oils.

answer.model_answer_md: A **fatty acid** has a **carboxyl group** attached to an R group, a hydrocarbon chain of 1 to 19 carbons: **palmitic acid** has 16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon. Fatty acids are **saturated** (no double bond) or **unsaturated** (one or more C=C bonds). **Glycerol** (trihydroxy propane) esterified with fatty acids gives **mono-, di- and triglycerides**; **oils** have low melting points and stay liquid in winter, while **fats** are solid. **Phospholipids**, such as **lecithin**, contain phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound and occur in membranes.

questions.solution_md: Fatty acids, glycerides, phospholipids, fats vs oils.

questions.stem_md: Describe how the chemical composition of living tissue is analysed, and summarise the main classes of compounds found in the acid-soluble pool.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Analysis.** A living tissue is ground in **trichloroacetic acid** with a mortar and pestle to give a thick slurry, which is strained through cheesecloth. The **filtrate** is the **acid-soluble pool** and the **retentate** the **acid-insoluble fraction**. Elemental analysis shows that living matter contains the same elements as the earth’s crust but in very different proportions: carbon and hydrogen are relatively far more abundant. Compound analysis reveals inorganic compounds (water, ions such as sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium, phosphate and sulphate) and organic compounds.

**Amino acids.** Organic compounds with an amino group and an acidic carboxyl group on the alpha carbon, plus hydrogen and a variable **R group** (H in glycine, methyl in alanine, hydroxymethyl in serine). They may be acidic, basic, neutral or aromatic, and their ionisable groups change with pH.

**Lipids.** Water-insoluble; fatty acids (palmitic acid with 16 carbons, arachidonic acid with 20), saturated or unsaturated; glycerol esterified to form mono-, di- and triglycerides (fats and oils); and phospholipids such as lecithin in membranes. Being membrane vesicles after grinding, lipids actually separate with the insoluble fraction.

**Nitrogen bases, nucleosides and nucleotides.** Adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil and thymine are bases; with a sugar they form nucleosides (adenosine, guanosine, thymidine, uridine, cytidine), and with phosphate added, nucleotides (adenylic, guanylic, thymidylic, uridylic and cytidylic acids).

**Metabolites.** Primary metabolites have identifiable functions; secondary metabolites such as pigments, alkaloids, terpenoids, essential oils, toxins, lectins, drugs and polymers like rubber are mostly of plant, fungal and microbial origin.

questions.solution_md: Method; amino acids, lipids, nucleotides, metabolites.

questions.stem_md: The most abundant protein in the whole biosphere is
questions.solution_md: RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere; collagen is the most abundant in the animal world — option (a).

It digests proteins in the gut

questions.solution_md: GLUT-4 is a transport protein for glucose; trypsin digests, antibodies fight infection and collagen forms ground substance — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A protein is made of four separately folded polypeptide chains, two of one kind and two of another, held together in a fixed arrangement. This arrangement is its
questions.solution_md: The assembly of several folded polypeptides, as in adult haemoglobin (2 α + 2 β), is quaternary structure — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The primary structure of a protein is

options.text_md: the right-handed helix formed by parts of the chain
its sequence of amino acids, from the N-terminal to the C-terminal amino acid
the folding of the chain into a ball

questions.solution_md: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence; the first is the N-terminal, the last the C-terminal amino acid — option (b).

options.text_md: two carboxyl groups, with addition of water
the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, with loss of water
the R groups of two amino acids

questions.solution_md: The –COOH of one amino acid reacts with the –NH2 of the next by dehydration — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a nucleic acid, a phosphate links the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ carbon of the next sugar. This link is a
questions.solution_md: An ester bond on each side of the phosphate makes a phosphodiester bond — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A drop of iodine solution turns a slice of potato blue-black but leaves a piece of cotton wool unchanged. Why?

options.text_md: Cotton contains no glucose at all
Iodine reacts only with proteins in the potato
Cellulose dissolves iodine and removes the colour
Starch forms helices that can hold iodine, but cellulose does not have such complex helices

questions.solution_md: Iodine sits in the helical parts of starch; cellulose, though also a glucose polymer, cannot hold it — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The hard shell of a crab is built of a complex polysaccharide containing amino-sugars. This polysaccharide is
questions.solution_md: Arthropod exoskeletons are made of chitin, built from chemically modified sugars — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A purified nucleic acid sample contains ribose and the base uracil. The sample is most likely
questions.solution_md: RNA has ribose and uracil; DNA has 2′-deoxyribose and thymine — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two DNA samples of equal length are heated. Sample X, rich in G–C pairs, needs a higher temperature to separate its strands than sample Y, rich in A–T pairs. Why?

options.text_md: G–C pairs are joined by peptide bonds
Sample X has more phosphodiester bonds between its strands
G pairs with C through three hydrogen bonds, while A pairs with T through two
A–T pairs are joined by covalent bonds that melt first

questions.solution_md: More hydrogen bonds per pair hold G–C-rich strands together more strongly — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose.

**Reason (R):** Cellulose forms complex helices that hold iodine and give a blue colour.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false, because cellulose has no complex helices and does not hold iodine (starch does) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the secondary structure of proteins, only right-handed helices are observed.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a polysaccharide chain such as glycogen, the right end is called the reducing end and the left end the non-reducing end.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: Match each protein (column I) with its function (column II).
questions.solution_md: Collagen forms ground substance, trypsin is an enzyme, insulin a hormone and antibodies fight infection.

questions.stem_md: How many peptide bonds are there in a single, unbranched polypeptide chain of 51 amino acids?
questions.solution_md: One fewer bond than residues: $51 - 1 = 50$ peptide bonds.

questions.stem_md: An unbranched chain of starch is built from 400 glucose units. How many water molecules were removed in forming its glycosidic bonds?
questions.solution_md: One water per glycosidic bond: $400 - 1 = 399$ water molecules.

questions.stem_md: Glycine has a molecular mass of 75 daltons and water 18 daltons. What is the molecular mass of a tripeptide made of three glycine units?
questions.solution_md: Two peptide bonds release two water molecules: $3 \times 75 - 2 \times 18 = 225 - 36 = 189$ daltons.

questions.stem_md: A short DNA segment has 6 A–T pairs and 4 G–C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
questions.solution_md: $6 \times 2 + 4 \times 3 = 12 + 12 = 24$ hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem_md: Give four functions of proteins, naming one protein for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Proteins act as **enzymes** (trypsin), **hormones** (insulin), **structural** material (collagen, the intercellular ground substance), **defence** (antibodies fight infectious agents), **transport** of nutrients across membranes (GLUT-4 carries glucose into cells) and **receptors** for smell, taste and hormones.

questions.solution_md: Any four functions with examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the four levels of protein structure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Primary:** the **sequence** of amino acids, from the **N-terminal** to the **C-terminal** amino acid.

**Secondary:** parts of the chain are arranged as a **helix** (only **right-handed** helices occur in proteins); other parts are folded in other forms.

**Tertiary:** the long chain is **folded upon itself** like a hollow woollen ball, giving the 3-D shape needed for many biological activities.

**Quaternary:** several folded **polypeptides** (subunits) are assembled, as in adult haemoglobin with **two α and two β** chains.

questions.solution_md: Four levels.

questions.stem_md: Name the polysaccharide that makes up most of (i) a sheet of paper, (ii) the grains in a potato tuber, (iii) the food store in liver and muscle, and (iv) the outer covering of a cockroach, stating its building blocks.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Cellulose**, a homopolymer of **glucose**; paper is made from plant pulp.

(ii) **Starch**, a polymer of **glucose**, the energy store of plants.

(iii) **Glycogen**, a branched polymer of **glucose**, the animal food store.

(iv) **Chitin**, a **complex polysaccharide** (heteropolymer) of **amino-sugars** and chemically modified sugars such as glucosamine.

questions.solution_md: Cellulose, starch, glycogen, chitin.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure and functions of the three main classes of biomacromolecules: proteins, polysaccharides and nucleic acids.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Biomacromolecules** have molecular weights above ten thousand daltons and are found in the acid-insoluble fraction.

**Proteins** are **polypeptides**, linear chains of amino acids joined by **peptide bonds**, formed by dehydration between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. There are 20 kinds of amino acids; those the body cannot make are **essential** and must come from the diet. A protein is a **heteropolymer**. Its structure has four levels: **primary** (sequence from N- to C-terminal), **secondary** (right-handed helices and other folds), **tertiary** (chain folded like a woollen ball) and **quaternary** (several subunits, as in haemoglobin with 2 α and 2 β chains). **Polysaccharides** are long chains of sugars joined by **glycosidic bonds**. **Cellulose** is a homopolymer of glucose forming plant cell walls, paper and cotton; it cannot hold iodine. **Starch**, the plant food store, forms helices that hold iodine and turn blue. **Glycogen** is the animal store, and **inulin** is a polymer of fructose. In a chain the right end is reducing and the left non-reducing. **Chitin** of arthropod exoskeletons is a complex heteropolymer of amino-sugars.

**Nucleic acids** (DNA and RNA) are **polynucleotides**. Each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base (purines adenine and guanine; pyrimidines cytosine, uracil and thymine), a pentose (ribose or 2′-deoxyribose) and a phosphate. Nucleotides are joined by **phosphodiester bonds**. In the **B-DNA** double helix of Watson and Crick, two antiparallel strands are held by hydrogen bonds, A with T (two) and G with C (three); one turn has ten base pairs and is 3.4 nm long.

- **Prosthetic groups:** organic compounds **tightly bound** to the apoenzyme, such as **haem** in peroxidase and catalase.
- **Coenzymes:** organic compounds bound only **transiently**, during catalysis; many contain **vitamins**, as **NAD and NADP** contain **niacin**.

questions.stem_md: What are enzymes? Explain how they speed up reactions and how temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors affect their activity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Enzymes** are biological catalysts. Almost all are **proteins** with a tertiary structure that forms an **active site**, a crevice or pocket into which the substrate fits; some nucleic acids, **ribozymes**, also act as enzymes. Unlike inorganic catalysts, which work best at high temperatures and pressures, most enzymes are damaged above about 40 °C, although enzymes of organisms in hot springs stay stable at 80–90 °C. Enzymes enormously raise reaction rates: carbonic anhydrase makes about 600,000 molecules of carbonic acid a second, compared with about 200 an hour without it.

**How they work.** Every reaction, even one that releases energy, must pass through a high-energy **transition state**; the energy needed is the **activation energy**. An enzyme binds its substrate (**induced fit**) to form an **enzyme–substrate complex**, which lowers the activation energy, so the substrate is converted to product much faster; the enzyme is released unchanged.

**Temperature and pH.** Each enzyme has an **optimum temperature** and **optimum pH**, with lower activity on either side. Low temperature keeps the enzyme temporarily inactive; high temperature **denatures** it.

**Substrate concentration.** Velocity rises with substrate concentration and then reaches **Vmax**, because all enzyme molecules are occupied.

**Inhibitors.** A **competitive inhibitor** resembles the substrate and competes for the active site, as **malonate** inhibits succinic dehydrogenase by mimicking succinate; such inhibitors are used to control bacterial pathogens.

questions.stem_md: Describe the six classes into which enzymes are divided and explain the role of cofactors, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Classes.**
1. **Oxidoreductases (dehydrogenases):** catalyse oxidation–reduction between two substrates, transferring hydrogen or electrons from one to the other.
2. **Transferases:** transfer a group other than hydrogen from one substrate to another.
3. **Hydrolases:** hydrolyse ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds; trypsin is an example.
4. **Lyases:** remove groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.
5. **Isomerases:** inter-convert optical, geometric or positional isomers.
6. **Ligases:** link two compounds together, forming C–O, C–S, C–N or P–O bonds.

**Cofactors.** Many enzymes need a **non-protein** part, the **cofactor**, to be active; the protein part is the **apoenzyme**, and activity is lost when the cofactor is removed. **Prosthetic groups** are organic and tightly bound — haem in peroxidase and catalase, which break hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, is part of the active site. **Coenzymes** are organic and bound only transiently during catalysis; they serve many enzymes, and many contain **vitamins** — NAD and NADP contain niacin. **Metal ions** form coordination bonds with the active site and the substrate — zinc is the cofactor of carboxypeptidase.

questions.solution_md: Six classes; three cofactors.

questions.stem_md: A student says: “Reaction rates double for every 10 °C rise, so salivary enzyme will digest starch about eight times faster at 67 °C than at 37 °C.” Evaluate this prediction, and describe a fair experiment to test it.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Where the claim comes from.** For ordinary chemical reactions the rate roughly **doubles for every 10 °C rise**, so a 30 °C rise would give a factor of 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Within a safe range, enzyme-catalysed reactions also speed up with temperature, because molecules collide more often and more readily reach the transition state.

**Why it fails here.** Salivary enzyme is a **protein** with an **optimum temperature** close to body temperature. Above about 40 °C human enzymes are **damaged**: heat **denatures** the protein, its tertiary structure and **active site** lose their shape, and the substrate can no longer bind. At 67 °C the rate would therefore be far **lower**, not eight times higher, and the loss would not recover on cooling. Only enzymes from organisms of very hot habitats stay active near 80–90 °C.

**A fair test.** Mix equal volumes of the same starch solution with the same amount of enzyme at a fixed pH, in water baths at, say, 17, 27, 37, 47, 57 and 67 °C. At timed intervals add a drop of the mixture to **iodine**; record the time for the blue colour to disappear. Keep all other conditions constant and repeat each temperature.

**Expected result and judgement.** The rate rises to a peak near 37 °C and falls steeply above it. The prediction is **wrong** because it applies a rule for uncatalysed reactions to an enzyme without allowing for denaturation.

questions.solution_md: Rule, denaturation, experiment, judgement.
